canvas-01.description: An inset in the lower left corner of the title and index sheet, showing the hamlet of Robanna, noted as located one and a half miles west of the Williamstown post office, at 50 feet to an inch. It is the only part of sheet 1 drawn to a fixed large scale; the key map of Williamstown above it is at about 500 feet to an inch and is not georeferenced. Public Road, thirty feet wide, runs from top to bottom through the middle of the inset and meets the Atlantic City Railroad (Philadelphia and Reading Railway) near the top edge, where the line runs east and west with a switch track on its south side. North of the tracks stand the small Robanna passenger station with its platform and, to the east, a freight platform. South of the railroad the inset shows open land in blocks 101 and 102: a brick dwelling with a pump west of Public Road, a corn crib, wagon house and hen house, a few frame outbuildings, and a dwelling and outbuilding east of the road. The note on the inset says there is no exposure on any side. Lot frontage numbers are given along both sides of Public Road.
notes: Public Road is today Tuckahoe Road, which runs north and south as drawn.
The railroad is the abandoned Atlantic City Railroad line, now the Harrison G. Shaw Bike Trail.

Placed from one hand-picked point (Public Road at the main track) with the scale of the 50 ft sheets and the angle of Tuckahoe Road and the trail; the printed north arrow points about 15 degrees west of the drawn road and was not used. Low confidence.
Printed on sheet 1, the title and index sheet; canvas label 'Index'.

Printed sheet 1: water facilities text, key map of Williamstown at about 500 ft to an inch (not configured), street and specials index, location map. Bottom-left inset ROBANNA at 50 ft to an inch (1.5 miles west of the post office): Public Road crossing the A.C.R.R. and P. & R. Ry. at the Robanna passenger station; configured as canvas-01 (one part, the inset only).

sheet-2.description: The north end of the built-up town of Williamstown, drawn at 50 feet to an inch with the sheet turned so that North Main Street runs straight up the page and north lies toward the upper right. The sheet covers North Main Street from the junction of Clayton Road, Sicklerville Road, Glassboro Road and Main Street at the bottom edge north to the top of the sheet, where it continues on the sheet above. Main Street is labelled 53 feet wide, with a six-inch water pipe down its middle. Glassboro Road leaves the main junction toward the upper left as a diagonal street, with narrow lots of 18 and 25 to 27 feet frontage laid out on its southwest side, and the sheet also shows the first block of Clayton Road to the west and of Sicklerville Road to the east, which runs off the right edge. Curtis Avenue, a fifty-foot street, meets Glassboro Road at the left edge. Most of the sheet is open ground with scattered frame dwellings and outbuildings set on long, narrow lots running back from Main Street. The principal non-dwelling buildings are the Grange Hall, on the north side of Clayton Road, a private truck garage on the northeast side of Glassboro Road, a gasoline station at the corner of Main Street and Sicklerville Road, a printing shop on Main Street, a cooperative, a junk storage shed, and a concrete-block garage for thirty cars on Sicklerville Road, heated by steam and lit by electricity, with an earth floor and pilastered concrete-block walls. Hydrants are marked by dots on the street lines. Sheet 3 adjoins at the bottom, and other sheet numbers are printed in the margins; a Map Division stamp of Princeton University Library overprints the bottom margin.
notes: North Main Street is today North Main Street north of the Clayton Road junction and South Main Street south of it; the Main Street junction with Clayton, Sicklerville and Glassboro Roads is one modern node.
Clayton Road is today Clayton Avenue; Curtis Av is today Curtis Avenue; Glassboro Road is today Glassboro-Williamstown Road (probable; the junction with Main matches the modern node).
The scale bar reads 50 feet to one inch and the fitted scale is 8.0 pixels per foot, as on sheet 3.
Curtis Avenue meets Glassboro Road at the sheet's left edge, off the image, so only the Main Street junction could be used as control.

North Main Street north of Clayton Road; Glassboro Road, Clayton Road (500 block), Sicklerville Road, Curtis Av at the left edge. 50 ft (bar read). Open ground; only the Main / Clayton / Sicklerville / Glassboro junction is usable: anchored on it (same junction as sheet 3), low confidence.

sheet-3.description: The centre of Williamstown, drawn at 50 feet to an inch with the sheet turned so that Main Street runs straight up the page (north lies to the upper right). The sheet covers Main Street from its junction with Clayton Road, Sicklerville Road and Glassboro Road at the top, where North Main Street begins, south to Hall Street at the bottom. Garwood Avenue crosses the upper half from west to east, Church Street enters from the west and Poplar Street from the east a short way apart in the lower half, and Clinton forms the eastern edge, with the start of Brooklyn Road in the lower right corner. The frontages along Main Street are mostly two- and two-and-a-half-storey frame dwellings and stores; the west side north of Garwood holds an auto repair shop and show room, a garage storing farm implements and autos, a junk shed and a concrete-block garage for thirteen cars. South of Garwood on the west side stand the Methodist Episcopal church with its seventy-foot tower and Sunday school, with a cemetery on both sides of Church Street behind them, and the post office near the bottom. On the east side of Main near Hall Street is the town hall and fire department, a brick and concrete-block building. A shirt factory stands on the north side of Poplar Street. The rest of the area is residential lots with frame dwellings and auto sheds, laid out in long narrow lots running back from Sicklerville Road, Garwood Avenue, Poplar Street and Hall Street, and two short private lanes labelled Drive. Water pipes of six and eight inches run under Main, Garwood, Church, Poplar and Clinton.
notes: Main is today North Main Street north of Clayton Road and South Main Street south of it; the junction of Main, Clayton Road and Sicklerville Road is one modern node.
Clayton Road is today Clayton Avenue.
Garwood Avenue is today East Garwood Avenue and West Garwood Avenue on either side of South Main Street.
Church, Poplar, Hall and Clinton are today Church Street, Poplar Street, Hall Street and Clinton Avenue.
Glassboro Road is probably today's Glassboro-Williamstown Road; its junction with Main was not used as control.
Clinton Avenue at East Garwood Avenue is two modern nodes 25 m apart; neither was detected.
Downtown: Main St from Clayton Rd/Sicklerville Rd to Hall St; Garwood Av, Church, Poplar, Hall, Clinton (east edge). 50 ft. Pilot sheet.

sheet-4.description: The commercial centre of Williamstown, drawn at 50 feet to an inch with the sheet turned so that Main Street runs straight up the page and north lies toward the upper right. The sheet covers Main Street from Hall Street at the top edge south to Chestnut Street near the bottom, with Washington crossing it about midway and Clinton forming the eastern edge. Blue Bell Road leaves Main Street near the top and runs diagonally toward the lower left, crossing the western half of the sheet; a block of lots with frame dwellings lies between it and Main Street, and a similar fan of long, narrow lots fills the upper left. Along Main Street stand the town's principal buildings: the Washington Hotel (heated by steam, lit by electricity and gas) with a bar, the First National Bank with a hall on the second floor, Rammels Hall with a restaurant and pool room below, a free library, a moving picture theatre with an asbestos projection room, a bus station and storage for auto busses, two garages, stores, and a temporary town hall. A fire department building stands on Blue Bell Road, and a water department pump house with a gasoline engine and a reservoir lies at the lower left on the line of an eight-inch water main. Hall Street Public School and a row of coops and sheds stand near the top right, and a large vacant building and a blacksmith shop lie east of Main Street south of Washington. The east and south of the sheet are largely open ground with scattered dwellings, private driveways and outbuildings. Water pipes of six and eight inches run under Main Street, Washington, Hall, Clinton and Blue Bell Road, and hydrants are shown by dots. The scale bar at the lower left reads 50 feet to one inch.
notes: Main is today South Main Street here.
Washington is today Washington Avenue east of Main Street; its western continuation, unnamed on the sheet, is Library Street today.
Hall, Chestnut and Clinton are today Hall Street, Chestnut Street and Clinton Avenue; Blue Bell Rd is today Blue Bell Road.

The Hall Street junction with Main Street lies at the top edge of the sheet and was placed from one drawn edge of Hall Street (boundary arm, with the width set to 38 feet as labelled); its point sits about 2.5 m south of the centre of the labelled pipe crossing.
The Clinton Avenue junction with Hall Street (right edge, top) was not detected and is controlled by sheet 3.
Main from Hall to Chestnut; Washington (west leg is Library Street today), Blue Bell Rd, Clinton on the east edge, Drive and private driveways. 50 ft (bar read).

sheet-5.description: The railroad crossing and the middle of Williamstown, drawn at 50 feet to an inch with the sheet turned so that Main Street runs straight up the page and north lies toward the upper right. Main Street crosses the sheet from Chestnut at the top, past Linwood Avenue, over the Atlantic City Railroad (the Philadelphia and Reading Railway), to Virginia Avenue and Carroll Avenue, and runs off the bottom edge toward Walnut on sheet 6. The railroad enters from the upper left in several converging tracks and leaves to the right as a single right of way with tracks in a twelve-foot cut. The freight house and passenger depot stand on the north side of the tracks, west of Main Street. North of the tracks, west of Main, lie the grist mills and lumber yards of M. D. Crane, with feed house, coal bins and coal pile, a lumber storage shed, and the A. Carino grist mill with its truck garage. East of Main Street the First Presbyterian Church, with a fifty-five foot tower, stands beside a cemetery that runs off the top right, and a long shed lies on Linwood Avenue. South of the tracks, a concrete-block walled works labelled Crew Levic Co. with gas tanks stands on Virginia Avenue, and the Catholic church and school of St. Mary's stands near the bottom left of Main Street. Elsewhere the sheet is residential, with frame dwellings on long narrow lots, private driveways, coops and outbuildings. Shisler Avenue forms the left edge, with only its east side drawn. Six- and eight-inch water pipes run in Main Street, Chestnut, Linwood, Virginia and Carroll. The scale bar at the bottom right reads 50 feet to one inch.
notes: Main is today South Main Street here; Chestnut, Linwood Av, Virginia Av, Carroll Av and Shisler Av are today Chestnut Street, Linwood Avenue, Virginia Avenue, Carroll Avenue and Shisler Avenue.
The sheet has no scale bar in the strip at the foot, but a 50 foot bar is printed at the lower right; it measures 8.0 pixels per foot, as on the neighbouring sheets, and the fit gives 7.88.
Control is weak: all junctions but two lie along Main Street, and the two Shisler Avenue junctions sit on the sheet edge (leave-one-out error about 5 m).
Shisler Avenue is lettered on the left margin; its centre lies about 300 pixels inside the edge of the scan.
The railroad is lettered A. C. R. R. (P. & R. Ry), and Railroad Right of Way, Tracks in 12 ft Cut; no running railroad survives in the modern reference data, so no rail crossings were used.
Main from Chestnut across the Atlantic City R.R. (depot) to Carroll Av; Linwood, Virginia, Carroll, Shisler Av, Walnut. 50 ft (bar at lower right). Four of six points on Main; scale weakly fixed.

sheet-6.description: Sheet 6 covers the southern end of the built-up area of Williamstown along South Main Street, which runs down the page. Walnut Street comes in from the right near the top, drawn 38 feet wide, and the map is bounded above by sheet 5, to the left by sheet 7 and below by sheet 10. West of Main Street, at the top left, the drawing shows the plant of C. D. Tice and Son, Coal, Wood, Ice and Cold Storage, with the ice factory, engine room, ammonia tanks and ice houses coloured as brick and fireproof construction, together with a wagon and auto shed, hydrants and a private water main. The company's stables and a wagon shed stand on the east side of Main Street. Below this the sheet is sparsely built: a single row of frame dwellings, mostly two and a half storeys with porches, lines the east side of Main Street, with a few more houses and small outbuildings on the west side set within long lots that run back from the street. A bottling works stands in the middle right of the sheet. Dashed lines mark six inch and two inch water pipes along Main Street and Walnut Street, and hydrants are shown as black dots. The lower two thirds of the sheet is mostly blank paper, with isolated dwellings strung along the street. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch, carries a north arrow at the right and the January 1930 Williamstown stamp.
notes: Main is South Main Street today; Walnut is Walnut Street.
Walnut Street is drawn 38 feet wide east of Main Street and jogs about 60 feet in position where it meets Main; the part west of Main (50 feet wide) is not in OpenStreetMap.
Georeferenced from the Main Street and Walnut Street junction alone, with scale and rotation taken from sheet 3: low confidence.
South Main Street south of Walnut. 50 ft. Walnut / Main is the only junction: anchored on it, low confidence.

sheet-7-1.description: The south-western part of Williamstown at 100 feet to an inch, with north towards the upper right. Oak and Centre cross the top of the sheet and Chestnut its upper middle, all running from the arbitrary Ames Road on the left edge eastwards to Blue Bell Road, which crosses the sheet diagonally from the lower left to Washington at the top right corner. The Atlantic City Railroad (Philadelphia and Reading Railway) curves through the sheet from the top left to the right edge, with a group of sidings and an iron trestle south of Chestnut. South of the railroad, Virginia Avenue runs east from Blue Bell Road, and the lower half of the sheet is a newly platted tract: Carroll Avenue and Walnut, partly marked not opened, crossing Shisler Avenue, with rows of narrow empty lots and almost no buildings. The built-up part is in the upper right: frame dwellings along Oak, Centre and Chestnut, the Allen A.M.E. Church and The Mission on Centre and Oak, a cluster of dwellings and stores around Blue Bell Road near Chestnut, the A. Carino grist mill with long sheds beside the tracks, a building for packing of produce, a shirt factory on Blue Bell Road and a builders' supplies, hay and grain storehouse on Virginia Avenue. The lower left corner of the sheet is taken up by an inset at 50 feet to an inch (part 2) showing works on Railroad Avenue elsewhere in town; this part is the rest of the sheet.
notes: Centre is today Center Avenue; Oak, Chestnut and Walnut are Oak Street, Chestnut Street and Walnut Street.
Ames Road is marked as an arbitrary name and is not in today's street data.
Carroll Avenue and Walnut are partly marked not opened in 1930.
The railroad is the abandoned Atlantic City Railroad line, now the Harrison G. Shaw Bike Trail west of town.
The junction of Blue Bell Road and Chestnut was detected about 5 m from the fit and left out; Blue Bell Road / Virginia Avenue was not detected.
A. Carino grist mill beside the railroad.

Main part at 100 ft: Oak, Centre, Chestnut, Ames Rd, Blue Bell Rd, the railroad, Virginia, Carroll, Walnut, Shisler Av. Bottom-left inset at 50 ft (printed): Railroad Av with the C. A. Raab catsup works, Kurzius and Friederich cider mill and pickle works, J. V. Sharp Canning Co.; part 2. Part 2 has no junction: placed from one point carried from sheet 8 (along the track from two building corners, across it from the Railroad Avenue hydrant; the hydrant alone disagrees with the buildings by about 6 m along the track), with sheet 8's rotation (the rails are drawn vertical on both) and the printed 50 ft scale. Low confidence, a few metres along the track.

sheet-7-2.description: An inset in the lower left corner of sheet 7, at 50 feet to an inch (twice the scale of the rest of the sheet) and drawn with north towards the upper right, showing the industrial strip on the west side of Railroad Avenue, where the Atlantic City Railroad runs beside the road. Railroad Avenue and the double track of the railroad form the right side of the inset; the inset continues the area of sheet 8, which draws the east side of the avenue. From north to south it shows the catsup and canning factory, paint shop and bottling works of Charles A. Raab, Inc., with a washery, storage and salt houses, a packing and canned-goods building and a boiler room; the cider mill and vinegar works of E. Kurzius and Henry Friederich and, south of it, their pickle factory, operated summer and fall only; and the works of the J. V. Sharp Canning Company, with a receiving shed, unloading shed, tomato preparing room, can storage and can making rooms, a bulk shed, engine and fire pump rooms, a coal pile, a separate warehouse and a storage shed, operated summer and fall only and fenced to the south. Notes give the power, heating, lighting and fire equipment of each works. A platform and scales stand by the tracks.
notes: Printed scale 50 ft to an inch; the main part of sheet 7 is at 100 ft.
Charles A. Raab, Inc., catsup and canning factory; E. Kurzius and Henry Friederich cider mill, vinegar and pickle works; J. V. Sharp Canning Co.

Main part at 100 ft: Oak, Centre, Chestnut, Ames Rd, Blue Bell Rd, the railroad, Virginia, Carroll, Walnut, Shisler Av. Bottom-left inset at 50 ft (printed): Railroad Av with the C. A. Raab catsup works, Kurzius and Friederich cider mill and pickle works, J. V. Sharp Canning Co.; part 2. Part 2 has no junction: placed from one point carried from sheet 8 (along the track from two building corners, across it from the Railroad Avenue hydrant; the hydrant alone disagrees with the buildings by about 6 m along the track), with sheet 8's rotation (the rails are drawn vertical on both) and the printed 50 ft scale. Low confidence, a few metres along the track.

sheet-8.description: Sheet 8 shows the western edge of Williamstown at 100 feet to an inch. A railroad runs down the left side of the page, and Railroad Avenue follows its east side from Clayton Road down to Church. Clayton Road crosses the upper part of the sheet from left to right, and Church runs across the lower part on a slight upward slope to the right. Between them lie three blocks of narrow building lots, laid out by Maple Avenue and Bodine Avenue and divided by lanes marked "not opened"; most of these lots are still empty, with dwellings concentrated along Railroad Avenue, Clayton Road and Church. Two Williamstown Public School buildings stand in the middle of the sheet, one beside Bodine Avenue and one east of it, both coloured as brick and heated and lit by steam or hot air and electricity. East of Bodine Avenue, Cameron Street and Garwood Avenue bound a large undeveloped tract, with the cemetery lettered across a large block below Garwood Avenue. At the upper left, beside the railroad, the Elec. Co. Office stands behind a switch house and transformer yard, and further left on Clayton Road is the packing house of Angelo Simei, with a cement-floored packing house, produce and auto sheds. A coop and a few dwellings and sheds stand on the west side of the tracks below Church. At the bottom, Oak runs with a row of dwellings on its north side, Ames Road crosses it marked as arbitrary, and the lower right corner shows the junction of Blue Bell Road and Washington Street with dwellings on the angled blocks. A north arrow stands at the top centre. Adjoining sheets are numbered 7 (left and bottom), 2 (top right), 3 (right) and 4 (bottom right).
notes: Clayton Road is Clayton Avenue today; Garwood Avenue is West Garwood Avenue; Church is Church Street; Cameron is Academy Street; Oak is Oak Street.

Railroad Avenue here (beside the railroad, from Clayton Road to Church) is not the modern Railroad Avenue, which lies on the east side of town; the railroad bed is now the Harrison G. Shaw Bike Trail and Sykesville Road starts where Church meets it.
Ames Road is lettered 'Arbitrary' and is not an existing street in the modern data.
Maple Avenue and Bodine Avenue are drawn only as far as Clayton Road and Church, and cross lanes marked 'not opened'.
A station building is lettered 'Church St. Station' on the railroad at Church.

West side at 100 ft: Clayton Road, Garwood Av, Church, Railroad Av beside the railroad (no modern street; the bed is the bike trail and Sykesville Road), Maple Av, Cameron (today Academy Street), Bodine Av, Oak, Ames Rd (arbitrary); Blue Bell Rd / Washington St in the bottom right corner. Drawn about 6 degrees from sheet 3 (square to its own streets). No control in the lower third.

sheet-9-1.description: The eastern side of Williamstown at 100 feet to an inch, drawn with north towards the upper right. Clinton runs down the left edge of the sheet from Poplar Street and Hall Street to Washington, and Madison Avenue runs parallel to it from Washington south to Linwood Avenue and Nassau Place. Brooklyn Road leaves Clinton at Poplar Street and runs diagonally to the lower right, meeting the eastern end of Washington at a small triangular block, from which Winslow Road runs south across the railroad and the road continues east to the unopened Acton Road at the right edge. The Atlantic City Railroad (Philadelphia and Reading Railway) crosses the bottom of the sheet on an embankment. Housing is thin: frame dwellings and auto sheds line Clinton, Madison Avenue, Linwood Avenue, Washington and Brooklyn Road, with large undivided tracts between them and several numbered blocks left almost empty. The water company's pumping station stands on the north side of Washington near Madison Avenue. Along the railroad at the foot of Madison Avenue and Nassau Place is the plant of the Alart and McGuire Company: a warehouse, a catsup and pickle factory with tomato washery and steamer, packing, bottling and shipping buildings, and a separate pickle manufactory, operated in summer only. The top right corner of the sheet is taken up by an inset (part 2) showing the Williamstown Foundry further east along Brooklyn Road; this part is the rest of the sheet. Six-inch water pipes run under Clinton, Poplar Street, Hall Street, Washington, Madison Avenue, Linwood Avenue and Brooklyn Road.
notes: Brooklyn Road is today Poplar Street east of Clinton Avenue and New Brooklyn Road beyond South Black Horse Pike; the Black Horse Pike, which now crosses the sheet from top to bottom, is not drawn.
Clinton and Washington are today Clinton Avenue and Washington Avenue.
Nassau Place and Acton Road are marked arbitrary names; Acton Road is marked not open. Neither is in today's street data.

The small triangle where Brooklyn Road, Washington and Winslow Road meet is drawn much smaller than the modern triangle of New Brooklyn Road, Washington Avenue and Winslow Road; those junctions were not used as control.

The railroad is the former Williamstown and Delaware River Branch, now abandoned; today's Railroad Avenue runs along its bed. Its crossing with Winslow Road was hand-picked as control for the east half of the sheet.
Alart and McGuire Company catsup and pickle works on the railroad, operated in summer only.

East side at 100 ft: Clinton, Brooklyn Rd, Washington, Madison Av, Linwood Av, Nassau Pl, Winslow Rd, Acton Rd, the railroad (Alart and McGuire catsup works). Top-right inset (part 2): Williamstown Foundry on Brooklyn Rd at Acton Rd.

sheet-9-2.description: An inset in the top right corner of sheet 9, at the same scale of 100 feet to an inch and drawn at the same angle as the rest of the sheet, separated from it by a heavy border. It continues Brooklyn Road east beyond the unopened Acton Road, whose junction with Brooklyn Road appears in the upper left corner of the inset and is also drawn at the right edge of the main part of the sheet. Brooklyn Road crosses the inset diagonally towards the lower right, with a six-inch water pipe along it and a few frame dwellings and outbuildings on its north side in block 73. South of the road, in block 74, lies the works of the Williamstown Foundry Company, noted as temporarily shut down: a long concrete-block foundry building with cupola and blower room, a sand house, a machine shop and pattern storage building and a sand and scrap storage shed, with a watchman but no clock. A siding of the Atlantic City Railroad (Philadelphia and Reading Railway) runs along the bottom of the inset past the foundry. The rest of the inset is open land.
notes: Brooklyn Road is today New Brooklyn Road.

The railroad is the former Williamstown and Delaware River Branch, now abandoned.

sheet-10-1.description: Part 1 of sheet 10 is the left side of the sheet, a long narrow strip of the northern end of North Main Street in Williamstown at 100 feet to an inch. North Main Street runs straight down the page, about 55 feet wide with a six inch water pipe laid along its east side, and is lined by house numbers in the 700s. Long building lots run back from both sides of the street, divided by thin lot lines, and most of them hold a single dwelling with a barn, shed or coop; a few small buildings are coloured as concrete block, and a store or two stands near the street. The only cross street on the part is Saybrook Avenue, which leaves North Main Street towards the right near the bottom of the part with a row of numbered lots along each side, one at the end marked vacant, and continues beyond the dividing line into the next part of the sheet. The notation 'No Exposure' is lettered along the upper edge, where the drawing stops short of the sheet border. The right side of the part is bounded by the heavy vertical line that separates it from parts 2 and 3, close to a printed compass rose, and the part joins sheet 2 at its foot. The area is open, with wide gaps between buildings, and a hydrant or two on the street.
notes: North Main is North Main Street today; Saybrook Avenue is Saybrook Avenue.
Placed from the North Main Street and Saybrook Avenue junction alone (scale and rotation from the sheet 8 and sheet 3 fits): low confidence.

Three parts at 100 ft separated by heavy lines at x = 3904 (full height) and y = 5962 right of it: part 1 (left) North Main Street north end with Saybrook Av, anchored on that junction; part 2 (top right) South Main Street south end (St. John's Lutheran Church), no junction, carried from sheet 6 at the match line; part 3 (bottom right) Sicklerville Road and Clinton east of sheet 2, Garwood at the bottom, one junction plus three parcel corners.

sheet-10-2.description: Part 2 of sheet 10 is the upper right of the sheet, a strip along the southern end of Main Street in Williamstown, at 100 feet to an inch. It continues sheet 6, whose number is lettered at the top left, and shows Main Street running straight down the page, about 50 feet wide, with a six inch water pipe in it. House numbers on the street are in the 800s with newer numbers in the 100s beside them. On the east side of the street the lots are regular and narrow; one of them holds St. John's Evang'l Luth'n Church, a concrete block building with a 38 foot tower heated by steam and lit by electricity, and the others hold dwellings, small sheds and a few coops. On the west side, behind a long block outlined by a thin line, stand a number of poultry houses ('coops'), two dwellings and sheds, set well back from the street. No cross street is drawn on the part. The 'Williamstown N.J. Jan 1930' stamp lies at the top right, and the part is bounded below by the heavy horizontal line that separates it from part 3 and on the left by the heavy vertical line that separates it from part 1. Most of the area is blank paper, as the town thins out into farmland towards the south.
notes: Main is South Main Street today.
St. John's Evang'l Luth'n Church is drawn here on the east side of Main Street.

No street junction is drawn on this part. It is placed from one point, where Main Street meets sheet 6 (carried from sheet 6), with scale and rotation taken from the other 100 foot parts: low confidence along the street.

sheet-10-3.description: Part 3 of sheet 10 is the lower right of the sheet, at 100 feet to an inch, east of the part of North Main Street shown on sheet 2. Sicklerville Road crosses the part from left to right on a slight upward slope, 43 feet wide west of Clinton and 37 feet wide east of it. Clinton, 30 feet wide, leaves Sicklerville Road at the left and runs down the page; at the bottom Garwood Avenue, 43 feet wide, meets it from the left, with a six inch water pipe laid in it. The blocks beside Sicklerville Road and Clinton hold a scattering of dwellings with barns and coops, numbered 601 to 612 on the west and 606 and 607A on the east. East of Clinton, on a long lot, stand a pair of barns and a dwelling, and further east is the milk dairy of H. H. Simmermon, with a milk house, a coop and a dwelling. The lettering 'No Exposure' runs along the right edge, where the drawing stops short of the sheet border. The rest of the part is blank paper, with the plate numbers of adjoining sheets 2, 3 and 16 and 73 (24) printed in it. A printed scale bar and the Princeton University Library stamp occupy the bottom edge. The part is separated from parts 1 and 2 by heavy black lines.
notes: Sicklerville Road is Sicklerville Road today; Clinton is Clinton Avenue; Garwood Avenue is East Garwood Avenue.
